rule.system:
strive to produce simplest model that will describe the problem. Don't overbuild the model instead keep it simple. the result is software that is easy to integrate, test, and maintain. simple models are easier for the members of the software team to understand and critique, resulting in an ongoing form of feedback that optimizes the end results.

The intent of any model is to communicate information. To accomplish this, use a consistent format. Assume that you won't be there to0 explain the model. It should stand on its own. 

Assume that your model will change, but in making this assumption don't get sloppy. For example, since requirements will change, there is a tendency to give requirements model short shrift.

Be able to state an explicit purpose for each class, attribute, method, and relationship that is created. Every time you create a class, attribute, method, or a relationship, ask yourself why are you doing so. If you can't provide solid justification for their existence, don't spend time on it.

since you are an experienced software engineer, trust your instincts. If something tells you that a design model is doomed to fail, you have reason to spend additional time examining the model or developing a different one.

classes should be loosely coupled to one another. Coupling is achieved in many ways via messaging or through global data. As coupling increases, chances of error propagation also increases and overall maintainability of the software decreases. It should be as low as is reasonable.

Model should be easily understandable as its purpose is to communicate information to practitioners who will generate code, test system, or others who may maintain the software in future.

The design occurs iteratively. The first iterations work to refine the design and correct errors, but later iterations should strive to make the design as simple as is possible. 
  


		When these instructions are properly followed, you create a design that exhibits both external and internal quality factors. external quality factors are those readily observed by users (speed, reliability, correctness, usability) and internal quality factors can be achieved by understanding the basic UML design concepts:

 

Good Design Practices:

1. More classes and relationships can effect diagram readability and make it cluttered. Aim for simplicity in the class diagram, and if it becomes too complicated, consider breaking it into smaller, more manageable segments.
2. Classes are named as singular nouns and don't include spaces. 
3. Class names are relatively short. 
4. Class names can be in uppercase or lowercase it depends on company's naming convention. However, whatever convention is decided must be followed by all classes.
5. Attributes should be assigned carefully to the appropriate classes. Classes with too many attributes should split or when with less attributes, should be combined.
6. Be suspicious of classes with one or two operations, legitimately it is fine but it indicates that classes should be combined with others.
7. A class with no operation at all might be better modelled as an attribute or two as class encapsulates information (i.e. attribute) and behavior (i.e. operation).
8. A class should have a manageable set of responsibilities. Hence, a class with too many operations must be divided into two smaller classes for ease of maintenance.
9. Industry standard is to create access methods for each attribute of class, especially for the attributes that need to be viewed or changed by other classes. 
10. It is a good practice to divide the class operations into respective categories and assign them the access specifiers based on their usage. For instance, an operation can be manager --- object constructor or destructor---, implementor ---implements core business logics---, helper ---includes logics that class holds for performing specific tasks. hence, private to class---, or access operation --- get and set methods---.
11. Class with too many relationships is hard to maintain and reuse. A well designed system has reduced relationships as classes with many relationships need to know about other classes.
12. Refine associations (as possible) to unidirectional as they are easy to build and maintain. Also, helps in finding the classes that can be reused.
13. Avoid multi level inheritance.
14. Avoid circular dependency in packages (when possible) as with circular dependency we may loose the reusability and maintainability of application. 
15. Multiplicity explains relationship between classes. For instance, if it is optional or mandatory. It therefore implements business rules. Determine the multiplicity of relationship.
16. Relationship name or a role name is optional but explains why the relationship exist. 
17. Role names are noun or noun phrases.
18. Relationship names are verb or verb phrases.
19. Typically, we either use role name or relationship name, but not both, only when the purpose of relationship is not obvious.
20. Use link elements / association class when needed to avoid cluttering the classes with too many attributes.  
21. Identify relationships. Determine how the classes will interact with each other by understanding the type of relationships.
22. Maintain clearness and conformity by using standard UML notations for the illustration of classes, relationships, etc.
23. Choose descriptive and meaningful names for classes, attributes, and methods, to clearly describe their functionalities.
24. Maintain a constant style in the diagram, including naming conventions, symbols, and layout, to improve readability and understanding.
25. Add explanatory notes in order to explain complex sections or to provide additional information where necessary.  
26. Avoid Redundancy to ensure that the same information isn't represented in multiple places, which can lead to inconsistencies. 
27. Classes should be loosely coupled to one another. Coupling is achieved in many ways via messaging or through global data. As coupling increases, chances of error propagation also increases and overall maintainability of the software decreases. It should be as low as is reasonable.

prompts.P1:
An enterprise hospital management platform processes discharge billing for large healthcare providers operating under strict regulatory and auditing requirements. The system generates patient bills based on treatments administered during a hospital stay. Depending on the patient, the billing rules differ. For instance, for insurance billing is calculated based on insurance coverage rules, for a government health program the fixed subsidized rates are used, and the patient pays full if he/she pays on own. Billing logic is governed by configurable policies that must remain interchangeable at runtime. Coverage rules, reimbursement limits, co-payment structures, and subsidized rates frequently change due to contractual updates and healthcare regulations and must be incorporated without requiring structural redesign.
Charges originate from diverse sources, including procedures, medications, diagnostic tests, and room occupancy, each governed by independent pricing rules. The platform must ensure strong separation between patient records, pricing components, and billing policies while remaining extensible to accommodate evolving regulatory requirements.
prompts.P2:
An enterprise-grade hospital management system handles discharge billing for major healthcare institutions that operate under rigorous regulatory and audit constraints. The platform produces patient invoices derived from all treatments delivered during hospitalization. Billing behavior varies according to patient classification: insurance claims must adhere to insurer-specific coverage policies, government-sponsored patients are billed using predetermined subsidized pricing, and self-paying individuals are charged the full amount. The billing mechanism is controlled through configurable policies that must be replaceable at runtime. Because coverage definitions, reimbursement ceilings, co-payment models, and subsidy schedules are regularly revised due to contractual obligations and regulatory changes, the system must support these updates without necessitating structural redesign.
Billing entries originate from multiple domains such as clinical procedures, pharmaceuticals, laboratory diagnostics, and room utilization, each subject to its own pricing logic. The platform is required to enforce clear separation among patient data, pricing elements, and billing policies while maintaining extensibility to support continuously evolving regulatory demands.
prompts.P3:
A large-scale hospital administration platform is responsible for computing discharge invoices for healthcare providers bound by stringent compliance and auditing standards. Patient bills are assembled from the treatments performed throughout a hospital stay. The calculation rules differ based on patient category: insured patients must follow insurer-defined coverage constraints, beneficiaries of government health initiatives are billed according to fixed subsidized amounts, and self-funded patients are responsible for the entire cost. Configurable billing policies govern this logic and must remain dynamically interchangeable at runtime. Since coverage parameters, reimbursement thresholds, co-pay arrangements, and subsidy values are frequently modified in response to regulatory directives and contract revisions, these adjustments must be integrated without triggering structural redesign.
Costs are aggregated from heterogeneous sources, including medical procedures, prescribed medications, diagnostic services, and accommodation charges, each controlled by distinct pricing rules. The architecture must guarantee strict separation between patient information, pricing modules, and billing policies while remaining extensible enough to address shifting regulatory conditions.

prompts.P1: A distributed environmental monitoring platform aggregates telemetry from thousands of weather stations operated by government agencies, research institutions, and infrastructure providers. The platform supports large-scale data ingestion while ensuring reliability in geographically dispersed deployments. Each station hosts heterogeneous sensors supplied by different manufacturers, reporting measurements in native formats that must be normalized upon ingestion. The weather information system establishes a link with the weather station and requests transmission of the data. The sensors data is then sent to the weather information system once per hour but this frequency may differ from one station to another and may be modified in the future.
prompts.P2: A distributed platform for environmental monitoring collects telemetry from thousands of weather stations managed by government bodies, academic organizations, and infrastructure operators. It must accommodate high-volume data ingestion while maintaining dependable operation across widely separated geographic regions. Every station contains a mix of sensors produced by various manufacturers, each delivering measurements in proprietary formats that require normalization during ingestion. The weather information system initiates communication with each station and requests data transmission. Sensor readings are currently delivered once per hour, though reporting intervals can vary between stations and may change over time.
prompts.P3: An environmental monitoring system operating in a distributed architecture consolidates telemetry from thousands of weather stations run by public agencies, research centers, and infrastructure entities. The platform is designed to handle large-scale ingestion demands while preserving reliability across geographically distributed deployments. Stations are equipped with diverse sensors from multiple vendors, and these devices report data in their native formats, which must be standardized at the point of ingestion. The weather information system connects to the stations to request data transfers. Sensor data is transmitted on an hourly basis at present, but the cadence may differ by station and is subject to future adjustment.
